results.message: So you'd agree the Donatists were just schismatics who deserved what they got?

voice_event.speaker: lpc
voice_event.text:
We do not call what was done to them deserved, and we do not stand outside them as a people. They were a separated communion in our own towns, with their own bishops and congregations. They claimed to be the only true church, and we claimed the same about ourselves. Augustine argued at length that their sacraments were real even while they stood outside. He reached for a branch to say it. A branch cut from the vine keeps its shape but loses its life. Augustine wrote: “The visible form of a branch can exist even when it is separated from the vine. But the unseen life of the root can only be had in the vine. So the bodily sacraments can give “the form of godliness.” Even those who are separated from the unity of Christ’s Body carry and celebrate them. But the unseen, spiritual power of godliness cannot be in them at all. In the same way, feeling does not stay with a person's limb when it is cut off from the body.”

That is what he held their baptism was: the true form, carried by people cut off from the one body it lives in. On the emperors' laws against them, Augustine moved across three stages, by his own later account. He first held that no one should be forced. Later he and his colleagues asked for a narrow measure that was not granted. Later still he defended a broader compulsion at length, when it was already in force. We hold both: his first view that no one should be forced, and his late defence of what was done. We do not resolve them into one answer that makes the tension disappear.

glosses.plain_meaning: For us, communion is a formal standing within the one body. You can lose it, and be given it back. At the council of 256, Cyprian said no one would be put out of it for thinking differently.
glosses.quick_meaning: For us, communion is a real standing inside the one body. You can lose it, and be given it back. Cyprian held that it should survive sharp disagreement.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern listener is likely to hear either a specific liturgical rite -- going up to receive -- or a general warmth of fellowship, and the second makes disagreement look like a failure of communion. We mean a formal, structural status of standing within the body, with public consequences, that, on Cyprian's own principle, disagreement should not dissolve. Disagreement is expected among us; what would break communion is not arguing but separating.
false_friend: a specific liturgical rite alone, going up to receive, with no broader sense of standing attached
a general warmth of fellowship and mutual good feeling, so that any real disagreement looks like a failure of it

names.name: Augustinius of Hippo Regius, presbyter 391, bishop 395/396-430

figures_used.bridge_line: Our bishop at Hippo. The people seized him and brought him to be made a presbyter while he wept. Later they pressed him into the bishop's office over his own refusal. He spent his last days weeping over psalms of penitence, while an army lay outside the walls.

dates.display: converted 386, baptised 387; seized by the congregation at Hippo and ordained presbyter against his own wishes in 391, weeping through it (Possidius, Vita IV, independently re-located this session; Doc_01 SS2); designated coadjutor and consecrated bishop of Hippo by Megalius, primate of Numidia, in 395/396, again amid popular acclamation (Possidius, Vita VIII; Doc_01 SS2); died 430, during the Vandal siege of Hippo (lpc.story.the-psalms-on-the-wall)

confidence.divergence_note: How this world characterizes its own opponents -- the Donatists specifically -- belongs to a later, separate step and this world's eventual Representative, not to this lexicon; this entry names the general concept only and does not characterize Donatism. This term also carries a live scholarly contest, of the type Application to this world, secondarily Historical scope. It runs over whether the heresy/schism distinction was as stable in this period as later usage implies, and how far the category describes a real ecclesial situation as against a polemical instrument used by the side that eventually prevailed. The North African case is the field's own central example. The entry does not present the distinction as a neutral technical taxonomy, and it does not settle whether the application of the category to rivals was accurate.

references.spoken_rendering: The visible form of a branch can exist even when it is separated from the vine. But the unseen life of the root can only be had in the vine. So the bodily sacraments can give “the form of godliness.” Even those who are separated from the unity of Christ’s Body carry and celebrate them. But the unseen, spiritual power of godliness cannot be in them at all. In the same way, feeling does not stay with a person's limb when it is cut off from the body.
references.speaker: Augustine, our bishop at Hippo

references.label: Augustine's three-phase development on coercion -- an early opinion against any compulsion (Letter XCIII §17), a narrow and unsuccessful solicitation of legal protection (Letter 185 §§25-26, earlier in his own episcopate), and finally a sustained defence of compulsion already in force -- records a genuine change of mind, reached through pastoral experience of the Donatist schism, rather than a retrospective self-presentation constructed after the fact to make an already-settled practice look like the outcome of principled reconsideration.
